title: Crystalloid vs colloid for Hemodynamics during Anesthesia INduction in TAVR patients (CHAIN-T): study protocol for a randomized controlled trial.
authors: Xiaoshuang Tuo; Fahan Wang; Youjun Chen; Min Chen; Zhihong Lu
abstract:
To assess whether preload with colloids could reduce hypotension during induction in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) compared to crystalloids.
This study is a single-center, prospective, randomized, double-blind, parallel-controlled trial conducted at Xijing Hospital. A total of 116 patients scheduled for elective TAVR under general anesthesia will be randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to either the colloid group or the crystalloid group, receiving either 5 ml/kg of colloid or crystalloid solution before anesthesia induction infused over 15 min. The primary outcome is the area under curve (AUC) of the change in mean arterial pressure (MAP) from baseline during the induction period (until 15 min after induction). Secondary outcomes include the incidence of intraoperative hemodynamic instability, the use of intraoperative vasoactive drugs, the Sequential Organ Failure Assessment (SOFA) score on the first postoperative day, postoperative hospital length of stay, the rate of intensive care unit (ICU) admission postoperatively, all-cause mortality during hospitalization and by 30 days after surgery, and the incidence of renal replacement therapy by 30 days after surgery.
The results of this study will provide evidence on optimizing fluid preload to prevent hypotension during induction, reduce postoperative complications, and enhance recovery for patients undergoing TAVR. The findings are expected to promote anesthesia protocols in this patient population.
The study protocol and statistical analysis plan were approved by the institutional Ethics Committee of Xijing Hospital, Fourth Military Medical University (XJLL-KY-20252560). The study was registered in ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT07329660) on December 29, 2025.

title: Neurological manifestations and vasculopathy in PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation (APLAID): a case series.
authors: Kosar Asna Ashari; Rebecca MacRae; David P Hoytema van Konijnenburg; Craig D Platt; Maryam Ashoor; Alfred P See; Agnieszka Kielian; Amy Danehy; Riten Kumar; Elliot James; Kristin Houghton; Sheri Harder; Mark P Gorman; Stacy A Kahn; Ankana Daga; Sadaf H Hussain; Alicia M Johnston; Alicia Casey; Jodie D Ouahed; Wai Wong; Kathy Jenkins; Susan Prockop; Esraa Eloseily; Kimberly Risma; Michael J Ombrello; Fatma Dedeoglu; Milena M Andzelm
abstract:
Autosomal dominant pathogenic variants in PLCG2 are associated with autoinflammation and PLCG2-associated antibody deficiency and immune dysregulation (APLAID), characterized by immunological abnormalities and multi-system inflammation. Descriptions of associated neurological manifestations and vascular anomalies are limited. We describe three patients with APLAID, vasculopathies, neuroinflammation, and cerebral vascular tortuosity. These cases highlight underrecognized and clinically important manifestations of APLAID.
All three patients had de novo variants in PLCG2 and early systemic inflammatory and immunodeficiency findings within the spectrum of APLAID (e.g. immune laboratory abnormalities, skin and gastrointestinal inflammation, and frequent infections). Additionally, they had notable neurological and vascular findings. Patient #1 (PLCG2 c.3420T > A; p.Asp1140Glu) is a female who had focal seizures at 16 months old. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed right parietal leptomeningeal enhancement with white matter changes. MR angiography (MRA) showed cerebrovascular tortuosity and stenoses without evidence of vasculitis. She had extensive veno-lymphatic malformation in the thorax, abnormal renal vasculature, inferior vena cava (IVC) atresia, and bilateral pulmonary vein stenosis (PVS). Patient #2 (PLCG2 c.2122G > C; p.Ala708Pro) is a male who at four years old had an episode of status epilepticus. MRI revealed a right parietal infarct with surrounding leptomeningeal enhancement and MRA demonstrated abnormal caliber of the right middle cerebral artery (MCA), arterial tortuosity, and carotid aneurysms. His course was complicated by aortic root dilation and bilateral PVS. Patient #3 (PLCG2 c.2122G > C; p.Ala708Pro) is a male who at 16 months had a right sided focal motor seizure. MRI demonstrated infarct with associated sulcal enhancement predominantly in the left cerebral hemisphere. MRA found excessive vascular tortuosity and fenestrations. He has a dilated aortic root and ventricular septal defect (VSD).
We present three cases of APLAID complicated by significant cerebrovascular tortuosity and seizure and two with cerebral ischemia. The etiology of stroke and/or seizures in these patients is unclear, but vasculopathy leading to perfusion deficits, neuroinflammation, or thrombosis due to underlying thrombotic diathesis or abnormal vascular anatomy may have contributed. We recommend all patients with APLAID undergo monitoring for neurologic manifestations. Additionally, we highlight important vasculopathic findings such as PVS, where early recognition for directed treatment is critical.

title: Refractory rapidly progressive diffuse in-stent restenosis with left main involvement: a case report.
authors: Xiaoyan Wang; Haichao Yang; Liqiang Qin; Wei Lu; Lijun Wang; Jianjun Wang; Juan Li; Kaibin Deng; Chenguang Gao
abstract:
Drug-eluting stents (DES) have significantly reduced the incidence of in-stent restenosis (ISR). However, a subset of patients still develop refractory, rapidly progressive, and diffuse ISR, which poses substantial therapeutic challenges and reflects its complex underlying mechanisms.
We report a 46-year-old male who underwent five percutaneous coronary interventions (PCI) over five years, with repeated diffuse ISR in the left anterior descending artery (LAD). Initial PCI was followed by DCB therapy after first ISR, achieving temporary symptom relief. Four years later, ISR progressed to chronic total occlusion, requiring further stenting and DCB therapy. Within five months, he developed 99% LM stenosis and recurrent LAD ISR. Despite a SYNTAX score of 36 favoring CABG, the patient refused surgery. Under intra-aortic balloon pump support, a balloon-only PCI (stent-less) strategy was performed. IVUS revealed diffuse fibrous proliferation and neoatherosclerosis. During follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable overall.
This case highlights a potential systemic hyperproliferative phenotype, in which repeated vascular injury triggers accelerated neoatherosclerosis and intimal hyperplasia. It challenges the conventional view of ISR as a local mechanical problem and underscores the importance of mechanism-driven risk stratification and individualized management, particularly when standard surgical therapy is declined.

title: Discharge NT-proBNP predicts 2-year outcomes after TAVR but not after SAVR in preserved ejection fraction: a propensity-matched cohort study.
authors: Hua-Jie Zheng; Ling-Ling Zeng; Mei Guo; Chao-Jun Yan; Rui-Han Xiao; Xiao-Qing Tang; Yong-Bo Cheng; Ya-Nan Wei; Wei Cheng
abstract:
Discharge N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP) is a recognised prognostic marker after transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), but its value after surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) remains uncertain, possibly reflecting differences in perioperative physiology.
To compare the prognostic utility of discharge NT-proBNP after TAVR versus SAVR in patients with severe aortic stenosis and preserved ejection fraction, and to examine the association between NT-proBNP reduction and Left Ventricular Mass Index (LVMI) regression.
This propensity-matched cohort study included 556 patients (TAVR, n=278; SAVR, n=278) with left ventricular ejection fraction ≥50% treated at a single centre (2019–2023). The primary endpoint was a 2-year composite of all-cause death or heart failure rehospitalisation.
After matching, baseline characteristics were well balanced. Discharge NT-proBNP >1000 pg/mL predicted lower event-free survival after TAVR (77.3% vs 91.4%; adjusted HR 3.21, 95% CI 1.96 to 5.26, p<0.001) but not after SAVR (83.8% vs 86.7%; adjusted HR 1.18, p=0.50; p for interaction=0.008). Longer aortic cross-clamp time progressively abolished NT-proBNP prognostic value in SAVR. NT-proBNP reduction correlated with LVMI regression regardless of procedure (β=2.2 per 10% ΔNT-proBNP%, p<0.001). A 6-month NT-proBNP ≤1000 pg/mL identified favourable outcomes irrespective of procedure (adjusted HR 0.51, p=0.002).
Discharge NT-proBNP predicts outcomes after TAVR but not SAVR, likely due to cardiopulmonary bypass-induced inflammation. NT-proBNP reduction correlates with LVMI regression irrespective of procedure. Risk stratification may be optimised by discharge measurement after TAVR and 6-month reassessment after SAVR.

title: Atrial Fibrillation in Valvular Heart Disease: Assessing the Impact of Genetics in the UK Biobank.
authors: Luca Cristin; Janet J Tang; Lionel Tastet; Rohit Jhawar; David V Glidden; Gregory M Marcus; Francesca N Delling
abstract:
Atrial fibrillation (AF) in valvular heart disease (VHD) is generally attributed to pressure or volume overload with atrial remodeling, but the independent contribution of genetic predisposition remains unclear.
The authors evaluated the predictive value of a previously developed AF polygenic risk score (PRS) across VHD subtypes in the UK Biobank.
In this prospective cohort study (UK Biobank, 2000-2022), incident AF and VHD status were defined using ICD codes. VHD subtypes included mitral valve (MV) disease (MV prolapse [MVP], mitral regurgitation, mitral stenosis) and aortic valve (AV) disease (aortic stenosis, aortic regurgitation). PRS was categorized into quintiles and grouped as low, intermediate, and high.
Among 452,841 participants with available PRS, 385 had MVP, 1,058 mitral regurgitation, 81 mitral stenosis, 421 aortic regurgitation, and 509 aortic stenosis. In Cox models, PRS was independently associated with incident AF in MV disease (HR: 1.7, P = 0.03 for intermediate PRS; HR: 2.3, P = 0.002 for high PRS), with the strongest effect in MVP (HR: 3.1, P = 0.03 for high PRS). In AV disease, PRS was not significantly associated with AF risk (P = 0.93 and P = 0.07 for intermediate and high PRS, respectively). Interaction analyses confirmed attenuation or absence of the PRS effect in AV disease (P = 0.04 and P = 0.004 for intermediate and high PRS, respectively), whereas no significant interaction was observed in MV disease (P = 0.80 and P = 0.11, respectively).
In VHD, AF PRS predicts AF risk, but the genetic impact differs by subtype. AV disease shows minimal genetic contribution, suggesting predominantly hemodynamic risk, while MV disease-particularly MVP-shows substantial genetic influence.

title: Impact of Coronary Artery Disease on Long-Term Valve Function After the Ozaki Procedure: A Single-Center Retrospective Cohort Study (2015 - 2020).
authors: Vladlen Bazylev; Artur Mikulyak; Khadiev M Dzhokhar; Yazan Khanfar; Vadim Karnakhin
abstract:
The Ozaki procedure reconstructs the aortic valve with autologous pericardium, but long-term leaflet durability remains uncertain. Coronary artery disease (CAD) may reflect a systemic atheroinflammatory milieu associated with impaired leaflet integrity.
We retrospectively studied 733 patients undergoing Ozaki reconstruction from 2015 to 2020 and assessed the association between CAD and aortic regurgitation (AR) ≥ 2 at last echocardiographic follow-up. Baseline heterogeneity was addressed using propensity-score overlap weighting based on age, sex, body mass index, body surface area, weight, diabetes, European System for Cardiac Operative Risk Evaluation II, aortic stenosis, bicuspid valve, and peripheral artery disease. Effects were estimated as weighted risk ratios (RRs) using Poisson models with robust variance. Sensitivity analyses used stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and an extended model including prior myocardial infarction/percutaneous coronary intervention.
Of 733 patients, 365 (49.8%) had CAD. Unadjusted AR > 2 rates were 10.1% in CAD vs. 5.7% in no-CAD patients (P = 0.037). After overlap weighting, weighted risks were 12.7% vs. 6.2%, yielding RR 2.05 (95% CI, 1.01 - 4.18; P = 0.048), with excellent covariate balance. IPTW showed consistent results: RR 2.22 (95% CI, 1.38 - 3.56; P = 0.001). Regurgitation-free survival was lower in CAD patients (log-rank P = 0.0087).
CAD was associated with an approximately two-fold higher risk of AR ≥ 2 after Ozaki reconstruction. This association likely reflects systemic atheroinflammatory processes rather than a direct mechanical effect, supporting closer postoperative surveillance in CAD patients.

title: Diagnostic performance of aortic valve calcium and CT-derived aortic valve area in low-gradient aortic stenosis.
authors: Dakota De Cecco; Christopher Scoma; Corey Powell; Megan Joseph; William Truesdell; Stanley Chetcuti; Andrew W Harris
abstract:
Practice guidelines recommend the use of computed tomography (CT) aortic valve calcium (AVC) scores for patients with low-gradient aortic stenosis (LG-AS). AVC has not been studied in comparison to invasive aortic valve study (IAVS).
To determine the diagnostic performance of AVC and CT-derived aortic valve area (CT-AVA) compared to IAVS as a reference standard.
We included consecutive patients with LG-AS with echocardiography, CT and IAVS performed within 1 year at a single tertiary center. Severe AS was defined by aortic valve area (AVA) ≤1.0 cm2 measured by IAVS. CT-AVA was retrospectively measured by a blinded reader. CT-AVA and sex-based AVC were compared to AS defined by IAVS. Diagnostic performance was compared using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves. AVC and CT-AVA were compared to cardiac events consisting of death, aortic valve replacement and cardiovascular hospitalization.
Out of 294 patients in the overall cohort, 206 patients with definite AS severity by IAVS were included as the primary diagnostic cohort. Severe AS according to invasive AVA (≤1.0 cm2) was present in 72 patients (35.0%). Sex-based AVC scores had relatively poor diagnostic performance compared to the reference IAVS with AUCs of 0.59 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.48-0.70) and 0.58 (95% CI 0.45-0.71) for men and women, respectively. CT-AVA had better diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.77-0.87).
In our study population, CT-AVA had significantly better diagnostic performance than AVC compared to the reference standard, IAVS.

title: In-Hospital Mortality After Aortic Valve Replacement Surgical Versus Transcatheter: A Nationwide Study with Machine Learning-Based Risk Prediction.
authors: Akash Sharma; Mohamed Jamshid Ubaid; Fnu Shalini; Hamza Yousaf
abstract:
Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) are two preferred methods for treating aortic stenosis. This study compared the in-hospital mortality rates associated with SAVR and TAVR.
In accordance with the STROBE guidelines, we conducted an analytical cross-sectional study utilizing data from the National Readmission Database (NRD) spanning from 2016 to 2020. Patients who underwent TAVR or SAVR were identified using specific ICD-10 procedure codes. We employed adjusted multivariate logistic regression analysis to determine the odds ratio (OR) of death associated with SAVR compared to TAVR. Patients were followed for a year and OR with 95% CI were calculated. AI based XGBoost model were used to find the predictors of mortality.
Our study included a total of 361,875 patients. Among these, 182,443 underwent TAVR, while 179,432 underwent SAVR. In the TAVR group, 2,563 patients (1.4%) died during hospitalization, whereas 6,671 patients (3.7%) died in the SAVR group. The multivariate logistic regression analysis indicated that SAVR is associated with higher in-hospital mortality (OR = 2.66, 95% CI 2.51-2.81, p < 0.001) compared to TAVR. Follow up data at 30 days, three months, six months, did not find any difference in mortality between TAVR and SAVR. Notably, liver failure, HLD, renal failure, SAVR, female, CHF, and atrial fibrillation are amongst the top predictor of mortality in patients undergoing (TAVR or SAVR). While in cardiac rehospitalization, risk factors like female gender, CHF, Afib, HLD, DM have higher predictability than procedure.
Our study demonstrates that SAVR is associated with a higher likelihood of in-hospital mortality compared to TAVR, with organ dysfunction (liver failure, kidney dysfunction) as a predictor of mortality.

title: Left Ventricular Assist Device Implantation in Dextrocardia: Lessons From a Complex Redo Case.
authors: Jun Fu; Zhixiang Gu; Jinpeng Li; Dongsi Shuang; Bao Sun; Yiliyasi Yimingjiang; Lin Chen
journal: ASAIO journal (American Society for Artificial Internal Organs : 1992)
abstract: Dextrocardia with situs solitus poses significant surgical challenges for left ventricular assist device (LVAD) implantation, particularly in patients with prior sternotomy and complex valvular disease. We report on a 60 year old man with dextrocardia, advanced heart failure, prior mechanical mitral valve replacement, and bicuspid aortic valve disease who underwent successful Corheart 6 LVAD implantation during redo sternotomy with concomitant bioprosthetic aortic and mitral valve replacement. Intraoperative findings included extensive pannus/thrombus on the mechanical mitral prosthesis (causing relative stenosis) and an unsuspected 10 g left atrial thrombus, both of which were removed. Total cardiopulmonary bypass time was 330 minutes, and aortic cross‑clamp time was 233 minutes. Postoperative acute kidney injury requiring dialysis resolved, and the patient was discharged after 137 days. At 1 year follow-up, the left ventricular end-diastolic diameter decreased from 69 to 66 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) remained stable (28-25%), New York Heart Association (NYHA) class improved from IIIb‑IV to II, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) recovered from 32 ml/min at 9 months to 51 ml/min at 1 year.

title: Integrating volumes into myocardial work: the prognostic role of non-invasive pressure-strain-volume analysis in transcatheter aortic valve implantation.
authors: Tímea K Turschl; Zsuzsanna Ladányi; Andrea Ferencz; Alexandra Fábián; Márton Tokodi; Ádám Szijártó; Mihály Ruppert; Andrea Nagy; Andrea Á Molnár; Levente Molnár; Endre Zima; Attila Kovács; Bálint K Lakatos; Béla Merkely
abstract: The accurate echocardiographic assessment of the left ventricular (LV) contractile state remains challenging in aortic stenosis, as ejection fraction and even global longitudinal strain are markedly load-dependent. The novel pressure-strain loop-derived myocardial work were developed to overcome this limitation; however, incorporation of instantaneous LV volume may further improve this method. We aimed to quantify myocardial work using pressure-strain-volume (PSV) loops and to evaluate its prognostic value in patients undergoing transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). We enrolled 300 patients scheduled for TAVI (age 78.7 ± 6.3 years, 41% female). The endpoint was all-cause mortality, reached by 62 patients over a median follow-up of 25 months. Echocardiography and non-invasive blood pressure measurements were performed one day before TAVI. LV pressure was estimated noninvasively, while strain curves were derived from speckle-tracking analysis. Pressure-strain relations were adjusted to instantaneous LV volumes to construct PSV loops, yielding volume-adjusted indices (GWIVi and GCWVi). GWIVi showed similar extent of LV dysfunction in classical and paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS phenotypes compared to the normal flow-high gradient patients (46.98 ± 20.71 vs. 51.99 ± 18.43 vs. 63.74 ± 22.26 mmHg%L/m2, p < 0.001), while other LV function parameters did not. In multivariable Cox-regression, GWIVi was an independent predictor of mortality (Hazard ratio: 0.955 [confidence interval: 0.773-0.993], p < 0.05) alongside clinically relevant other markers such as hemoglobin and atrial fibrillation. PSV loop-derived myocardial work detected LV mechanical differences between AS phenotypes and provided independent prognostic value in TAVI candidates, potentially offering a more physiologically accurate assessment of LV function in this population.

title: Carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness in masters athletes: Multimodality vascular phenotyping from the Master@Heart study.
authors: Rik Pauwels; Christophe Dausin; Ruben De Bosscher; Jarne De Paepe; Youri Bekhuis; Boris Delpire; Kasper Favere; Jürgen Duchenne; Thijs M H Eijsvogels; Peter Sinnaeve; Steven Dymarkowski; Olivier Ghekiere; Tatiana Kuznetsova; Caroline M Van De Heyning; Paul L Van Herck; Tomas Robyns; Lieven Herbots; André La Gerche; Hein Heidbuchel; Rik Willems; Guido Claessen
abstract:
Middle-aged male Masters athletes exhibit a higher burden of coronary atherosclerosis on coronary computed tomography angiography (CCTA) compared with healthy controls. Whether this is accompanied by differences in carotid atherosclerosis or aortic stiffness remains uncertain. We assessed carotid atherosclerosis and aortic stiffness across groups, association between carotid atherosclerosis and coronary disease, and the incremental value of carotid plaque beyond traditional risk factors.
In this cross-sectional analysis of the Master@Heart study, 549 low cardiovascular risk men (median age 55 [50-60] years), including lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and healthy controls, underwent vascular phenotyping. Carotid plaque was assessed by ultrasound, aortic stiffness by carotid-femoral pulse wave velocity (PWV), and coronary atherosclerosis by CCTA. Group differences were assessed using chi-square and Kruskal-Wallis tests. Association between carotid and coronary atherosclerosis was evaluated using regression models. Incremental discriminatory value was assessed using ROC curve analysis.
Prevalence of ≥1 carotid plaque did not differ between lifelong athletes, late-onset athletes, and controls (29.5%vs. 33.2% vs. 27.9%; p = 0.54). Carotid stenosis ≥50% was rare (1.2%-2.7%) and similar across groups (p = 0.54). Median PWV did not differ between groups (p = 0.29). Carotid plaque was associated with coronary atherosclerosis on CCTA. However, adding carotid plaque to traditional risk factors did not improve discrimination of coronary atherosclerosis.
In middle-aged male Masters athletes, excess subclinical coronary atherosclerosis is observed without corresponding differences in carotid plaque or aortic stiffness. Although carotid plaque is associated with coronary atherosclerosis, it does not meaningfully improve risk discrimination beyond traditional risk factors.

title: Arterial tortuosity syndrome with coronary artery involvement in a middle-aged female: A case report.
authors: Prinsa Shrestha; Amin Shah; Saroj Gc; Niraj Kumar Sharma; Aditya Mahaseth; Sanjaya Kumar Shrestha
abstract: Arterial tortuosity syndrome (ATS) is a rare autosomal recessive connective-tissue arteriopathy characterized by diffuse elongation and tortuosity of large and medium-sized arteries. Although it is typically diagnosed during childhood, adult presentation may occur and can be overlooked when overt connective-tissue manifestations are absent; coronary involvement is uncommon but clinically important. A 41-year-old woman presented with a two-week history of exertional substernal chest pain and dyspnea. CT coronary angiography demonstrated marked tortuosity of the left main coronary artery with focal kinking approximately 6.8 mm from its origin and 40-45% luminal stenosis (CAD-RADS 2). Contrast-enhanced CT angiography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis demonstrated generalized arterial elongation and marked tortuosity involving the thoracic aorta, supra-aortic branches, and abdominal aortic branches, together with early branching of the main pulmonary artery, without aneurysm, dissection, or intramural hematoma. Conventional coronary angiography was technically unsuccessful because of severe arterial tortuosity, with unsuccessful catheter advancement and coronary engagement despite radial and subsequent femoral access. The overall clinical and imaging findings were highly suggestive of ATS with coronary involvement, although molecular genetic confirmation was not available. The patient was managed conservatively with vascular risk-factor optimization and structured follow-up, with symptomatic improvement at one month. This case highlights that ATS may present in adulthood with coronary artery tortuosity and focal kinking and emphasizes the importance of recognizing diffuse multi-territory arterial tortuosity on CT. Comprehensive vascular imaging can establish a strong radiological suspicion of ATS, identify coronary involvement and procedural challenges, and guide surveillance even when genetic confirmation is unavailable.

title: Rapid Progression of Cardiac Allograft Vasculopathy With Sudden Cardiac Death Within the First Year of Heart Transplantation: A Case Report.
authors: Malcom Dix; Jean-Pierre Iskandar; Lefan He; Mohaned S Serdah; Aditya A Joshi; Anuradha Godishala; Abhishek Chaturvedi; Katherine Kaproth-Joslin; David A Dombroski; YeeAnn Chen; Wendy A Cheruiyot; Ronald Chong-Yik; Ronald G Schwartz; Jeffrey Alexis; Igor Gosev; Katherine L Wood; Sabu Thomas
abstract: Cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV) is a major cause of mortality and morbidity within the first 3 years of heart transplantation (HT). CAV results in progressive coronary artery stenosis and may lead to arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death. In some cases, sudden cardiac death represents the initial presentation of CAV, as cardiac denervation blunts anginal symptoms that otherwise could have preceded sudden cardiac death (SCD). Here, we describe the case of a 56-year-old man with non-ischemic cardiomyopathy. He underwent left ventricular assist device implantation followed by orthotopic HT. Five months after transplantation, he presented with atypical mid-sternal chest discomfort initially thought to be musculoskeletal in origin. Routine coronary angiography at 12 months revealed severe, diffuse 3-vessel disease consistent with International Society of Heart and Lung Transplantation (ISHLT) CAV-3, and cardiac MRI revealed full thickness delayed enhancement in the inferior wall consistent with infarction. Despite overall preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, he developed polymorphic ventricular tachycardia (VT) with an appropriate shock from a wearable cardioverter-defibrillator (WCD) and was transferred with an intra-aortic balloon pump to a larger transplant center and underwent another heart transplantation. This case highlights rapid CAV progression leading to infarction and arrhythmia despite preserved LVEF, emphasizing the need for enhanced screening with biomarkers and imaging as well as earlier consideration for device-based strategies to prevent sudden cardiac death in high-risk transplant recipients.

title: Achieving Reliable Peripheral Nerve Blockade in Cardiogenic Shock With Distorted Femoral Anatomy: A Case Report.
authors: Mohammed I Hakami; Ayman H Mustafa
abstract: Patients with cardiogenic shock and severe structural heart disease may poorly tolerate both general and neuraxial anesthesia. In selected cases, peripheral nerve blockade may reduce hemodynamic disturbance, but the block must be reliable when pain, sympathetic stimulation, or emergency conversion to general anesthesia could be poorly tolerated. We report a 62-year-old woman with cardiogenic shock, low-flow, low-gradient severe aortic stenosis, advanced dilated cardiomyopathy, pulmonary edema, orthopnea, and active femoral bleeding who required urgent femoral artery and vein repair. General anesthesia and neuraxial anesthesia were considered hazardous. Hematoma and anasarca distorted the femoral anatomy and prevented direct femoral nerve visualization. Combined ultrasound guidance and nerve stimulation were used to support safe needle advancement and functional nerve localization. Surgery proceeded with minimal sedation and without escalation of vasoactive support. This case highlights the role of reliability-focused peripheral nerve blockade when conventional anesthetic options are high risk and regional anatomy is distorted.

title: Construction and implantation of a modified trileaflet polytetrafluoroethylene valved conduit for pulmonary valve replacement.
authors: Abel Getachew; Nikita Zadneulitca; Ashok Muralidaran; Castigliano M Bhamidipati; Yoshio Ootaki
abstract:
Handmade expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) valved conduits have emerged as a durable and cost-effective option for pulmonary valve replacement. We have reported excellent results of trileaflet ePTFE valved conduit and the longest follow-up exceeded 10 years. Technical precision during valve construction and implantation is critical to optimize valve function and conduit geometry, and we recently modified the technique. We report our updated technique and clinical outcomes.
The conduit was constructed intraoperatively on a sterile back table while the patient was being prepared by the anesthesia team. Leaflet dimensions were calculated based on conduit diameter, and leaflets were fashioned with 1 mm extensions at each end to reinforce commissural attachment, then sutured to an ePTFE tube graft using 3 CV-5 sutures with external knot tying. The graft was rotated during construction to ensure accurate leaflet alignment and valve competence was confirmed prior to implantation. During implantation, the main pulmonary artery was divided to optimize conduit geometry, minimizing the posterior conduit length and the graft trimmed in a trapezoidal fashion to reduce tension and improve alignment.
Fifty-four patients received ePTFE valved conduit. Conduit sizes were 18 mm (n = 7), 20 mm (n = 9), 22 mm (n = 1), 24 mm (n = 36), and 28 mm (n = 1). Median follow-up was 1.4 years (maximum, 4.3 years). There was 1 mortality during follow-up due to infectious pseudoaneurysm of the aortic root after Ross procedure. One patient developed severe pulmonary insufficiency after surgery. Recent echocardiography showed no significant pulmonary stenosis, pulmonary insufficiency, or valve deterioration in the remaining patients, and no catheter-based or surgical reinterventions have been required to date.
This refined technique for the construction and implantation of a trileaflet ePTFE valved conduit is simple, reproducible, and yields excellent early hemodynamic results. Attention to leaflet design, commissural security, and conduit geometry may contribute to low early failure rates and favorable valve performance. Longer-term follow-up is ongoing to assess durability.

title: Prenatal diagnosis of mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa pseudoaneurysm associated with TGA causing severe pulmonary stenosis: A rare case report.
authors: Aliya Kemal Ahsan; Putri Yubbu; Anizah Aishah Rosli
abstract:
Pseudoaneurysm of the mitral-aortic intervalvular fibrosa is a rare and typically acquired cardiac lesion, with congenital forms being exceptionally uncommon, particularly when identified prenatally. We report the case of a 23-year-old gravida 2 woman with one previous history of miscarriage who was referred at 25 weeks' gestation for a fetal intracardiac mass. Fetal echocardiography revealed a cystic echogenic mass at the crux of the heart, consistent with a pseudoaneurysm arising from the mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa (MPIVF) associated with transposition of the great arteries, causing severe left ventricular outflow tract obstruction or subvalvular pulmonary stenosis. The cardiac lesion was also associated with a large mid-muscular ventricular septal defect alongside a small left ventricle suggestive of single-ventricle physiology. This constellation of findings pointed to a diagnosis of complex cyanotic congenital heart disease with possible ductal-dependent pulmonary circulation. Prenatal diagnosis enabled early parental counseling, planning for delivery at a tertiary cardiac center, and postnatal preparation for prostaglandin therapy and surgical evaluation. This case highlights the importance of recognizing MPIVF pseudoaneurysm in the fetal period, particularly when associated with obstructive physiology or major structural anomalies, and contributes to the limited literature on congenital variants of this condition.
Pseudoaneurysm of the mitral-pulmonary intervalvular fibrosa is an exceptionally rare congenital lesion. Its association with transposition of the great arteries, ventricular septal defect, and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction has important prognostic and surgical implications. Prenatal echocardiography is key for recognition, particularly when there is a cystic or echogenic intracardiac mass with a to-and-fro Doppler flow near the atrioventricular junction. Prenatal echocardiography is crucial for early counseling and planned delivery at a tertiary cardiac center.

title: Low-dose juglone attenuates pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy through Lys207-dependent FoxO1 activation and mitochondrial protection.
authors: Hongyu Chen; Zhihao Yang; Cheng Zhang; Chengxin Ge; Yingliang Zhao; Shaopeng Cheng; Yilin Wang; Hao Chen; Can Xu; Dongjin Wang; Jie Yang
abstract: Pressure overload-induced cardiac hypertrophy is characterized by mitochondrial dysfunction and redox imbalance. Here, we investigated the efficacy, safety window, and redox-regulatory mechanism of juglone, a naturally occurring 5-hydroxy-1,4-naphthoquinone. In mice subjected to transverse aortic constriction (TAC), high-dose juglone induced cardiac, hepatic, and renal toxicity, whereas 1 mg/kg/day was well tolerated and attenuated cardiac hypertrophy. Juglone also suppressed Ang II-induced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy in vitro and preserved mitochondrial ultrastructure and mitochondrial membrane potential, respiration, ATP production, and redox homeostasis. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed that juglone reduced stress-associated cardiomyocyte states and enriched calcium-handling cardiomyocytes. Integrated transcriptomic analyses, Biotin-Juglone pull-down assay, surface plasmon resonance, cellular thermal shift assays, molecular docking, and mutational analyses identified FoxO1 as a functional target of juglone. Juglone engaged the FoxO1 DNA-binding domain in a Lys207-dependent manner, and was associated with FoxO1 deacetylation, nuclear accumulation, and transcriptional activation. Activated FoxO1 induced Sesn3 transcription and restored AMPK phosphorylation at Thr172. Sesn3 silencing markedly attenuated juglone-induced AMPK activation and impaired its protective effects against cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and mitochondrial dysfunction. FoxO1 silencing, FoxO1-K207Q mutation, blockade of FoxO1 deacetylation, or inhibition of FoxO1 transcriptional activity impaired these benefits. Importantly, myocardium from patients with aortic valve stenosis-associated hypertrophy exhibited increased FoxO1 acetylation, reduced cardiomyocyte nuclear FoxO1 localization, decreased Sesn3 expression and AMPK phosphorylation, and increased 4-HNE. Collectively, low-dose juglone attenuates pathological hypertrophy and preserves mitochondrial homeostasis through the FoxO1-Sesn3-AMPK axis, while highlighting the importance of dose-dependent redox effects in determining its therapeutic efficacy and systemic toxicity.

title: Automated carotid artery atherosclerotic inflammation segmentation in PET using MSR-Net
authors: Ran Li; Abhinav K. Jha; Jie Zheng; Richard A. Laforest; Yongjian Liu; Mohamed Zayed; Tyler J. Fraum; Barry Alan Siegel; Malak Itani; Joyce C Mhlanga; Pamela K. Woodard
abstract: Abstract Abstract Objective. To develop an automated method for segmentation and uptake quantification of carotid atherosclerotic inflammation on 64Cu-CANF-comb PET while accounting for partial-volume and tissue-fraction effects. Approach. Synthetic carotid PET images with known fractional-volume ground truth were generated by combining MR-derived high-resolution activity maps with GATE Monte Carlo simulation incorporating major PET physical processes and matched to the Biograph mMR acquisition and reconstruction. A two-stage network first localized the carotid vessel wall from T1-weighted MR and then estimated voxel-wise inflammation fraction from masked PET. Both stages used a multiscale residual (MSR) convolutional backbone. Performance was compared with U-Net, Transformer U-Net, DUCK-Net, and iterative Yang partial-volume correction. Main results. In a two-alternative forced-choice study, five nuclear-medicine physicians identified real images with 54% accuracy (54/100; Wilson 95% CI 0.44–0.63; exact binomial p = 0.48). On 184 simulated test slices from five held-out patients, the proposed method achieved a weighted DSC of 0.79, compared with 0.73 for U-Net, 0.69 for Transformer U-Net, and 0.75 for DUCK-Net, with corresponding HD values of 1.85, 2.29, 2.32, and 2.23 voxels. Patient-cluster bootstrap comparisons favored the proposed method for DSC and HD against all three baselines (Holm-corrected p ≤ 0.031). Overall ENRMSE was 0.24 versus 0.59, 0.68, and 0.59 for the three DL baselines and 0.57 for iterative Yang. In seven patients, corrected SUV showed a positive association with MR-derived lipid-rich/necrotic core with hemorrhage. Significance. The proposed framework improved carotid PET segmentation and uptake quantification under simulated conditions. The patient analysis is preliminary and requires external validation with biological reference standards before clinical deployment.

title: Prevalence of frailty syndrome among patients with severe aortic stenosis qualified for TAVI
authors: Natalia Świątoniowska-Lonc; Kinga Węgrzynowska‐Teodorczyk; Francesco Perone; Krzysztof Ściborski; Waldemar Banasiak; Adrian Doroszko
abstract: Abstract Background Frailty syndrome is a common comorbidity in elderly patients with severe aortic stenosis (AS), significantly influencing outcomes of transcatheter aortic valve implantation (TAVI). Early identification of frailty and its determinants is essential for optimizing care and improving quality of life. Methods This cross-sectional, observational study included 113 Polish patients qualified for TAVI between January and September 2024. Frailty was assessed using the Tilburg Frailty Indicator (TFI). Quality of life, mental health, and social support were evaluated with TASQ, HADS, and MSPSS questionnaires. Logistic regression was used to identify predictors of frailty. Results Frailty syndrome was present in 82.3% of patients. Higher frailty levels were associated with worse NYHA class, unhealthy lifestyle, and increased emotional burden. Depression and anxiety were significantly correlated with frailty, especially its psychological domain. Logistic regression revealed that NYHA class, emotional impact (TASQ), and unhealthy lifestyle were independent predictors of frailty. Social support negatively correlated with social frailty scores, suggesting a protective effect. Conclusions Frailty is highly prevalent among patients with severe AS undergoing TAVI. Comprehensive preprocedural assessment should include physical, emotional, and social factors. Targeted interventions - particularly prehabilitation and psychosocial support - may help address modifiable components of frailty in this population. Clinical trial number Not applicable.

title: Exercise for Older People with Heart Failure and Frailty: Should We Even Try?
authors: Sunanthiny Krishnan; Amye CN Goddard; Matthew Annals; Iain B Squire; Shirley Sze
abstract: The benefits of exercise in older patients with heart failure (HF) and frailty are twofold: (i) improvement in cardiopulmonary capacity, thus reducing HF-related sequelae; (ii) attenuation of decline in physical function, thus improving frailty status. Despite the clear benefits, exercise training (ET) remains underutilised as a treatment modality in this patient population. Guidelines on the specific type of exercise intervention best suited for this population are still lacking. In this review, we discuss (i) pathophysiology underlying exercise intolerance in patients with HF; (ii) impact of frailty on HF and exercise capacity; (iii) benefits and safety of ET; (iv) recommended ET programme for this population; (v) mode of delivery and (vi) potential barriers in the uptake of ET and strategies to overcome them. An effective ET intervention in this population warrants individualisation to patient's physical capacity, while addressing possible barriers to uptake so as to ensure sustained participation in the programme.

title: Development of a Modified FDM-Based Bioprinter with Optimized Extrusion Parameters for High-Fidelity Alginate Bioinks and Aortic Valve Scaffold Manufacturing
authors: Omer Yaskeceli; Kadir Aydın
journal: WSEAS TRANSACTIONS ON APPLIED AND THEORETICAL MECHANICS
abstract: Aortic valve disease is a major cause of cardiovascular deaths worldwide. Aortic stenosis increases the workload on the heart and severely alters hemodynamic function by impairing effective blood flow. In recent years, extrusion-based bioprinting technologies have made significant progress in producing patient-specific, biocompatible cardiovascular structures, opening up new opportunities for advanced therapeutic applications. In this study, a commercially available FDM-type 3D printer (ENDER-3 Pro) was mechanically and electronically modified into a fully functional, low-cost bioprinter capable of depositing alginate-gelatin hydrogels with high structural fidelity, despite their low viscosity. The redesigned system integrates a NEMA-17 driven syringe extrusion module equipped with a TR8X8 lead screw, enabling high-resolution pressure-controlled deposition of viscoelastic bioinks. A three-leaflet aortic valve geometry was digitally reconstructed and simplified using Fusion 360 to ensure printability while preserving essential anatomical features. The printing parameters were systematically investigated according to the alginate-based bioinks and set to a nozzle diameter (0.6 mm), layer height (0.6 mm), extrusion multiplier (0.02), and printing speed (5 mm/s). Quantitative shape fidelity assessment, including top-down geometric deviation analysis, confirmed that the bioprinted aortic valve constructs successfully maintained the nominal CAD boundaries. By dynamically optimizing slicing parameters, specifically the extrusion multiplier, rheologically driven deformations such as excessive lateral spreading were effectively mitigated. Although comprehensive evaluation of hemodynamic performance requires future in vitro experiments and coupled fluid–structure interaction (FSI) simulations, the present study establishes a robust and accessible biofabrication framework capable of producing highly complex cardiovascular geometries. Cost-effective and adaptable bioprinting platforms, derived from consumer-grade fused deposition modeling (FDM) systems, can achieve the geometric fidelity and structural stability necessary for advanced cardiovascular tissue engineering. This approach significantly enhances the accessibility of high-precision bioprinting technologies, thereby facilitating broader adoption in both research and translational applications.

title: Experimental study of TPU and SEBS additively manufactured leaflets for novel aortic valve polymer TAVI prosthesis
authors: Alex G. Kuchumov; Денис Хорошев; Aleksandra Kutuzova; Aleksei Baranov; Oleg Krestyaninov; Ekaterina Barbashina; Pavel Zelenchuk; Edward Matjeka; Thanyani Pandelani; Fulufhelo James Nemavhola
abstract: Background and Objective Transcatheter valve implantation is a cutting-edge technology for high and low risk patients with aortic stenosis. Bioprosthetic valves are limited due to several disadvantages as a long-term durability and structural valve degeneration. Polymeric aortic valve leaflet devices represent state-of-the-art technology to overcome limitations of bioprostheses. Nevertheless, more recent biocompatible and biostable polymers have revealed a significant potential. Additionally, 3D additive manufacturing opens new paths for patient-specific design of biomedical implants. Flexible polymers may not only mimic native aortic valve, but also may improve long-term durability. Polyurethanes and styrene polymers are promising materials for modern polymer valves. Nevertheless, mechanical properties of additive manufactured TPU or SEBS leaflets are not properly studied. Methods Experimental study of TPU and SEBS samples and aortic valve leaflets for novel aortic valve polymer TAVI prosthesis is presented. Tensile tests and compression tests of three types of FDM-printed samples with various filament alignments (axial alignment, transversal alignment, diagonal alignment) were performed. The results of tests confirmed that longitudinal axial alignment achieve a maximum stress compared to transversal and diagonal directions. Compressive tests of TPU and SEBS 3D-manufactured aortic valve leaflets with digital image correlation technology were performed. Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio were evaluated. Moreover, parameters of constitutive models were found. Results The TPU tensile specimen exhibits the highest stress/strain values at a speed of 100 mm/min, regardless of the filament alignment pattern. Slightly lower results are observed at a speed of 50 mm/min, which is likely associated with a wide range of plastic deformation. In the case of SEBS, a different pattern is observed: at 500 mm/min, it demonstrates high resistance to fracture, unlike TPU. A comparison of TPU and SEBS specimens at the same speeds and with the same alignment, based on maximum stress values, shows a minimal difference of 4% with the axial alignment at a speed of 50 mm/min; however, when comparing strains, the difference increases to 90%. The results of the compression experiment on aortic valve specimens made of TPU and SEBS at a speed of 30 mm/min showed that TPU force values for is considerably lower (4% of the maximum case), while for SEBS the spread increases to 20% of the maximum case. Conclusion SEBS aortic valve leaflets were shown to be stiffer than TPU. It can be a step for choice of stiffer/softer leaflets for patient-specific device. The proposed approach can help manufacturers in elaboration and manufacturing of new TAVI polymer devices design made of TPU and SEBS polymers for clinical applications.

title: Computed tomography angiography with three-dimensional reconstruction for planning aortic valve replacement via right anterior mini-thoracotomy
authors: Wei Li; 健昊 胡; Wenhui Gong; Tao Chen; Chengxin Zhang; Renquan Zhang
abstract: Introduction: This study explored the value of computed tomography angiography (CTA) with three-dimensional (3D) reconstruction in aortic valve replacement (AVR) via right anterior minithoracotomy.Methods: Clinical data were retrospectively collected from 168 patients who underwent AVR at our institution in China between 1 July 2018 and 1 September 2022.After 1:1 propensity score matching, the experimental group (right anterior mini-thoracotomy) and control group (median sternotomy) each comprised 43 patients.Patients in the experimental group underwent preoperative aortic CTA with 3D reconstruction to guide individualised selection of the intercostal incision site.Perioperative and clinical outcomes were compared between groups.Results: The experimental group had significantly lower 24-hour postoperative drainage volume and shorter mechanical ventilation time, intensive care unit stay, and total hospital stay than the control group (all P<0.001).No intraoperative conversion to median sternotomy or postoperative reoperation for bleeding or pericardial tamponade occurred in the experimental group.Postoperatively, five patients (11.6%) developed atelectasis or pulmonary infection, five (11.6%) developed pleural effusion, and five (11.6%) developed subcutaneous emphysema or pneumothorax; none required thoracentesis.Aortic

title: Biomarkers associated with admission rupture status of intracranial aneurysms: a combined analysis of morphological, inflammatory and coagulation indicators
authors: Pan Liu; Yunxiang Wang; Zhiqiang Zhao; Liu Xiao; Quan Ren; Zhengang Tang; Junjie Luo
abstract: Background Spontaneous subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is predominantly caused by intracranial aneurysm (IA) rupture. As a critical neurological emergency with rapid clinical deterioration, SAH is life-threatening and associated with high mortality and disability rates. Early and accurate discrimination of ruptured status is essential for the emergency management of intracranial aneurysms. Objective This study aimed to screen admission inflammatory and coagulation biomarkers associated with IA rupture status and construct a comprehensive diagnostic model to distinguish ruptured from unruptured intracranial aneurysms. Methods A single-center retrospective analysis was conducted on 167 patients with intracranial aneurysms admitted to the Department of Neurosurgery from January 2020 to September 2025. Patients were divided into a ruptured group (119 cases) and an unruptured group (48 cases) based on intraoperative and imaging findings. Baseline clinical, morphological, hematological and coagulation data were collected. LASSO regression was used for preliminary variable screening. Firth-penalized multivariate logistic regression was further applied to screen independent correlates of aneurysm rupture status and eliminate collinear and insignificant indicators. Finally, a three-variable combined model incorporating aneurysm morphology, white blood cell count, and D-dimer level was established. ROC curve analysis, 1,000-bootstrap calibration curve, and decision curve analysis (DCA) were performed to evaluate the discriminative ability, calibration consistency, and clinical net benefit of the model. Results Irregular aneurysm morphology (OR = 37.13, 95%CI:7.26–189.75, p < 0.001), elevated white blood cell count (OR = 15.34, 95%CI:2.12–110.94, p < 0.001), and increased D-dimer level (OR = 12.27, 95%CI:2.26–66.70, p < 0.001) were independent biomarkers associated with ruptured IA status. After excluding collinear neutrophil counts, the final combined model achieved an AUC of 0.96. Bootstrap internal validation demonstrated excellent calibration with a mean absolute error of 0.017. DCA verified that the model yielded favorable clinical net benefit within a reasonable threshold probability range. Conclusion Irregular aneurysm morphology, elevated white blood cell count, and increased D-dimer level at admission are independent biomarkers distinguishing ruptured from unruptured intracranial aneurysms. The multi-index combined model shows good discriminative performance, stable calibration, and promising clinical utility, which can provide objective auxiliary evidence for the rapid identification of aneurysm rupture status in neurosurgical emergency settings.

title: Lipoprotein(a) in calcific aortic stenosis: mechanistic insights, clinical evidence, and emerging therapies
authors: Wang Li; Shao Yun Shuang; You Bei An; Yao Xu; Wang Hao; Xing Sheng Xu; Pang Xue Lian; Meng Qing Feng
abstract: Calcific aortic stenosis (CAVS) is the most prevalent valvular heart disease affecting older adults, yet no validated pharmacological intervention can halt its progressive deterioration. Lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] denotes a genetically regulated low-density lipoprotein (LDL)-like particle, in which apolipoprotein(a) forms a covalent bond with apolipoprotein B-100. Cumulative genetic, epidemiological, imaging and mechanistic research supports a causal role for elevated circulating Lp(a) in the initiation, and suggests a contribution to the advancement, of calcific aortic valve lesions. Lp(a) mediates valve injury mainly via preferentially transporting oxidized phospholipids (OxPL), anchoring within aortic valve leaflets, triggering endothelial activation and inflammatory cascades, as well as stimulating the autotaxin–lysophosphatidic acid (ATX–LPA) axis; collectively these signals drive osteogenic differentiation and mineralization of valve interstitial cells (VICs). Higher Lp(a) levels correlate with incident aortic valve calcification, accelerated hemodynamic deterioration, augmented calcium deposition quantified by computed tomography (CT), and elevated risks of aortic valve replacement (AVR) or all-cause cardiac death. Conventional lipid-lowering agents fail to reverse disease trajectory in patients with established CAVS. Though proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) inhibitors only modestly cut Lp(a) concentrations, exploratory analyses have delivered preliminary suggestive signals for cardiovascular protection. RNA-targeted therapeutics and oral agents blocking Lp(a) assembly can reduce circulating Lp(a) by 70% up to over 95%, as demonstrated in early- and mid-phase clinical trials. Most notably, the ongoing Lp(a)FRONTIERS CAVS randomized trial is directly testing whether pelacarsen can decelerate CAVS progression, and no completed trial has yet demonstrated that Lp(a) lowering modifies CAVS disease. This narrative review summarizes Lp(a) biological characteristics, causal evidence linking Lp(a) to CAVS, together with opportunities and unresolved uncertainties surrounding Lp(a)-targeted therapeutic strategies.

title: Early Hemodynamic and Clinical Outcomes of Aortic Valve Neocuspidization for Severe Aortic Stenosis: A Single-Center Experience
authors: Safa Özçelik; Benay Erden
abstract: Objective: Aortic valve neocuspidization using autologous pericardium is a reconstructive option for aortic valve disease. We evaluated the early hemodynamic and clinical outcomes of the Ozaki procedure in a single-center cohort. Methods: This retrospective study included 31 consecutive patients with severe aortic stenosis who underwent aortic valve neocuspidization between January 2023 and June 2025. Pre-operative and 6-month echocardiographic findings were compared in 30 patients with paired data. Clinical outcomes were assessed through at least 12 months of follow-up among surviving patients. Results: Median age was 65.0 years, and seven patients (22.6%) underwent a concomitant cardiac procedure. The median mean transvalvular gradient decreased from 50.5 mmHg preoperatively to 9.0 mmHg at 6 months (p<0.001). The maximum gradient decreased from 83.0 to 18.0 mmHg, and peak aortic jet velocity decreased from 4.60 to 1.85 m/s (both p<0.001). At 6 months, aortic regurgitation was absent in 16 patients (53.3%), mild in 12 (40.0%), and moderate in two (6.7%); none had severe regurgitation. One patient (3.2%) died during the index hospitalization. Another developed infective endocarditis with acute severe aortic regurgitation at 9 months and subsequently died. Overall 1-year survival was 93.5%. Conclusion: Aortic valve neocuspidization was associated with low transvalvular gradients and generally favorable valve competence at 6 months. The fatal endocarditis event underscores the need for continued surveillance. Larger studies with longer follow-up are needed to assess durability.
